item.title: cloudflare/security-audit-skill
item.description:
A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

security-audit

A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness. The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

What it does

The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

  1. Reconnaissance -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json.
  2. Coverage-led hunting -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.
  3. Candidate validation -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.
  4. Structured output -- write confirmed, needs_validation, and rejected records to findings.json and validate them against report-schema.json.
  5. Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.
  6. Target-neutral reporting -- derive REPORT.md, FINDINGS-DETAIL.md, and NEEDS-VALIDATION.md from the verified records and coverage ledger.

The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs validate-findings.cjs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

The verdicts are distinct: confirmed has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, needs_validation has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and rejected records a disproved candidate.

Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

Files

File Purpose
SKILL.md Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns
RECONNAISSANCE.md Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions
HUNTING.md Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules
ATTACK-CLASSES.md Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts
MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets
AI-AND-LLM.md Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets
WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets
CLIENT-SIDE.md DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets
SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes
CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes
PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes
RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes
DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes
DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes
VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting
report-schema.json JSON schema for all three findings.json verdicts
validate-findings.cjs Zero-dependency validator for findings.json in Phases 4 and 5
validate-findings.test.cjs Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks
validate-coverage-ledger.cjs Zero-dependency validator for coverage-ledger.json in Phases 1–5
validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs Coverage-ledger validator tests

Installation

Install the skill with the Skills CLI:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit

Use --global for a user-level installation:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit \
  --global

Run npx skills --help for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

Usage

Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

security audit this codebase

find security vulnerabilities in ./src

do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>. The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

Requirements

  • A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents
  • Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators
  • An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as needs_validation instead of executing target code.

Design principles

  • Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as needs_validation with its exact unresolved fact.
  • Adversarial validation. The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.
  • Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.
  • Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.
  • Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

Contact

Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

item.title: Leonxlnx/taste-skill
item.description:
Agent skills that give coding agents taste: art direction, reference images and a browser check instead of generic AI pages

https://tasteskill.dev

     

Sponsors

interfaces.dev · A design engineering magazine by Jakub Krehel
React Bits · animated React components for creative interfaces
IMG.LY · CreativeEditor SDK
Sent.dm · messaging APIs for SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS

Become a sponsor

Taste Skill (tasteskill 2.5.1) is an Agent Skill that makes coding agents build professional company websites at the figma.com and x.ai level instead of assembling a generic landing page. Every build uses plain copy, one design system, one section per screen, equal left and right edges, real photographs (licensed stand-ins when the client has none), real brand icons and real product UI, a hero entrance and one or two dealt moments on every page, quiet micro-interactions, and shader effects and scroll scenes kept strictly for tech, gaming and software pages, all verified in a real browser by a checker and a finish gate that enforce the rules.

Pages built from a single brief in earlier v2 runs:

The photographs are real, found in open archives and credited by the skill (credits). Watch the launch film.

Install

npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "design-taste-frontend"

That installs the skill with the npx skills CLI.

The skill runs its scripts with Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge or Chromium (set CHROME_PATH if it is in a non-standard place). Optional: ffmpeg on the PATH, for WebP output and the phone crop of a hero photograph in photos.mjs. It installs nothing and needs no API keys. Bundled Wikimedia Commons photographs work offline; fetching additional photographs or icons uses network access.

Claude Code plugin

Run these inside Claude Code. The skill is namespaced under taste-skill:, so it does not collide with your other skills.

/plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill
/plugin install taste-skill@taste-skill

/plugin update upgrades it later.

Codex plugin 
codex plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill
codex plugin add taste-skill@taste-skill

Start a new Codex session afterwards so the skill is loaded.

From a clone, linked instead of copied

./install.sh symlinks the skill into Claude Code (--codex for Codex, --all-agents for both), so a git pull updates it in place. On Windows (Git Bash) it makes a real link, or a directory junction when symlinks are not allowed, and it reports an older copied folder instead of skipping it silently.

Already have the skill? Run the install command again; the install name did not change. Looking for one of the older skills? See Moved skills.

How 2.5 works

Use it by asking your agent to build or redesign a company site; the agent loads the skill, copies assets/ into the project, starts from assets/starter.html and runs the checker before it hands the page over. Every build starts by classifying the client's business (software, gaming, tech, product, service or place) and planning the page screen by screen before writing markup:

  1. Deal tokens and layout. scripts/start.mjs deals a palette made for the trade and a Google Fonts pairing for the page kind (library/palettes.json, library/type.json), and assets/layout/deal.mjs deals a hero layout (split, centred, product, photo, place, collage, editorial, word, film, statement or triptych).
  2. Start from one system. assets/starter.html, assets/system.css and assets/layout/layout.css enforce one section per screen at desktop (1440x900), equal left and right content edges, a fixed navigation bar and a single-screen closing footer (footer.closing).
  3. Show real product UI and real photographs. Software and tech pages populate lit feature cards (assets/ui/cards.css) with rewritten HTML UI fragments (assets/ui/) and node-and-line diagrams (assets/diagrams/), with real brand and interface SVGs resolved locally by scripts/icons.mjs. Place, shop, hospitality and non-technical product pages lead with curated photographs (scripts/photos.mjs, assets/photos/), typography and flat colour, crediting sources in one expandable footer line with no captions under images.
  4. Keep effects for tech and gaming pages. Shader grounds (scripts/effects.mjs), scroll scenes (assets/scenes/) and procedural 3D prints (assets/objects/) are dealt only on software, tech and gaming pages within a four-context WebGL cap, with static fallbacks for phones and reduced motion. Every page gets a hero entrance and one or two moments from scripts/moments.mjs; cafes, hotels, shops, studios and services get only the photo- and type-led ones, and zero WebGL.
  5. Check in a real browser over HTTP. scripts/consistency.mjs, assets/layout/check.mjs, scripts/perf.mjs and scripts/shoot.mjs render the built page in headless Chrome across 1440, 1024, 768 and 390, catching empty visuals, broken shaders, contrast drops, misaligned columns, section-height drift, placeholder text, invented street numbers and slow-network image gaps before the build ships. scripts/gate.mjs then holds the finish until no fixable FAIL is left, three rounds at most.

Details of what changed from 2.1.x are in the changelog.

The tools

Everything is a plain Node 22+ script in the skill folder; none installs anything.

Tool What it does
scripts/start.mjs Deals a palette and a Google Fonts pairing for the page kind and prints the <head> links and :root tokens.
assets/layout/deal.mjs Deals one of eleven tested hero layouts; assets/layout/check.mjs checks it with long-headline stress tests.
scripts/photos.mjs Deals vetted photographs by trade, enforces image weight and writes the one footer credit line.
scripts/icons.mjs Resolves real brand and interface icons into local SVG files.
scripts/effects.mjs, scripts/moments.mjs Deal shader grounds for tech, gaming and software pages, and the moments for every kind.
scripts/gate.mjs, scripts/copy-lint.mjs The finish gate (also a Stop hook) and the copy linter it runs.
scripts/consistency.mjs The checker: renders the page in headless Chrome over HTTP at 1440, 1024, 820, 768 and 390 and prints PASS, WARN or FAIL per rule.
scripts/perf.mjs, scripts/shoot.mjs Page weight and speed, and full-page and per-section screenshots.

First run, from the project folder (a deal also arms the finish gate there): node scripts/start.mjs deal --page software (kinds: software, gaming, tech, product, service, place). Check a built page with node scripts/consistency.mjs <url or file> --page <kind>.

Moved skills

This repo holds one skill, design-taste-frontend. The others moved to repos of their own and kept their install names:

Install name Where it lives now
high-end-visual-design, minimalist-ui, industrial-brutalist-ui, gpt-taste, stitch-design-taste, design-taste-frontend-v1, design-taste-frontend-v2-experimental Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics
imagegen-frontend-web, imagegen-frontend-mobile, brandkit, image-to-code Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills
redesign-existing-projects Part of design-taste-frontend, which audits an existing page in a real browser before changing anything
full-output-enforcement Removed. For the same problem, see Leonxlnx/unlazy

Install a moved skill from its new repo under the same name:

npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics --skill "high-end-visual-design"

Common Questions

What does the skill need?
Node 22 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium; ffmpeg is optional (WebP photographs and the phone crop of a hero photograph). It installs nothing and uses no API keys. Bundled Commons photographs are stored locally; network access is used only when downloading additional photographs, Google Fonts or brand icons.

Where do the pictures come from, and can I use them?
From the skill's vetted photograph library (assets/photos/photos.json, including bundled Wikimedia Commons WebP sets and Unsplash photographs) dealt by scripts/photos.mjs. Library frames are used for trade and material details (or marked explicitly as draft stand-ins when the client has no photographs yet), never passed off as the client's own room, staff or product, and credited in one expandable footer line (photos.mjs credits).

Does it work with React, Vue, Svelte, plain HTML?
An empty folder gets a static page from assets/starter.html. An existing React, Vue, Svelte, Astro or Tailwind project is built in its own stack, with the kit served from its public folder; a Next.js brief is built as a static export. The browser checks run on the served or built page.

When does a page get shaders or scroll effects?
Shaders only on software, tech (technical hardware) and gaming pages, and always within a four-context WebGL budget with static phone and reduced-motion fallbacks. Places, shops, cafes, hotels, studios, services and everyday physical products stay calm: photographs, sharp typography and flat colour, with a hero entrance and one or two photo- or type-led moments in their own sections.

item.title: DuarteSantos8/openGym
item.description:
Open-source gym & body-weight tracker, now in the App Store (iPhone + Apple Watch) and as an Android APK. Plan routines, log workouts, see which muscles are trained, import from Strong/Hevy/FitNotes. Self-host it or use it on the phone alone.

https://opengym.ch

Website · Live demo · Roadmap · Changelog

Why openGym

Most workout apps keep your data on their servers, push you towards a subscription, or vanish when the company does. openGym runs on your own box, keeps your data in a folder you control, and is yours to fork. It still behaves like a modern app: installable on the home screen, passkey sign-in, works offline, syncs between your phone and your laptop.

No account on someone else's server, no subscription, no ads, no telemetry. One docker compose up and it's running.

The in-browser demo is the real app with example data, if you want to try it before installing anything.

Features

Planning

  • A routine per weekday over a library of over 5,600 exercises with animated demos, searchable and browsable by muscle on a body map. Filter by the equipment you own.
  • Four starter plans (Push/Pull/Legs, Upper/Lower, Full Body, 5×5) that load as ordinary, editable routines.
  • Every session on the Plan page and today's on Home carries a tiny body map with the muscles it works lit up, so you know Leg Day is legs before you open it.
  • Move a session to another day without touching the weekly plan. The week starts on Monday or Sunday, your choice.
  • Or skip the weekdays altogether: a rotation (A, B, C, A, ...) where the next session is simply the next one you haven't done, however the week went.
  • Supersets, warm-up sets, drop sets and rest-pause, timed exercises (planks, hangs, carries), cardio by time and speed, rest time per exercise, planned deloads.
  • Your own exercises, with your own photo, GIF or short video. Location data is stripped on the device before upload.

Training

  • Guided sessions: today's workout starts itself, weights are pre-filled from last time, a rest timer runs between sets, PRs are detected as you go. On a rest day it tells you when the next session is.
  • A quiet workout screen: one menu per exercise, the set number as the set's own menu, card or list view. Switches in Settings bring the old button rows back if you liked them.
  • Optional effort column as RIR or RPE, colour-coded, with a plain-language line per level.
  • Plate math for barbell, EZ bar, trap bar and Smith machine, worked out from the plates you own. Train in more than one place? Each gym keeps its own plates, dumbbells, bars and machine stacks, and the phone can switch to the gym you just walked into.
  • Bodyweight exercises know they carry no load: log reps, add a dip belt if you use one.
  • Per-side reps for lunges and single-arm work, the screen stays awake while you train, and a rest-timer alert can flash the screen for loud gyms.
  • Swipe a set left to delete it (with Undo) or right to copy it. Pyramid sets with their own reps and rest per set, and a scroll wheel for any rest time up to 15 minutes, or no timer at all.
  • Machine taken? A planned backup exercise swaps in with one tap and keeps the slot's sets and reps. Machines can carry their real weight stack, odd steps included, and progression sticks to it.
  • The session's volume runs live at the end of the progress bar.

Progress

  • Progression rules per routine or per exercise: linear, Greyskull LP, double progression through a visible rep range, triple progression (reps, then sets, then load), or adding time. Each target explains why it is that number; missed reps never add load, stalls trigger a deload.
  • Estimated 1RM per exercise with its own curve, Structural Balance ratios (Poliquin, Thibaudeau, ATG), a year-long activity heatmap.
  • A muscle map in three modes: where your volume went, what is still recovering, and what has gone untrained.
  • Body-weight chart against a goal line, with your weekly rate and an optional lose, gain or hold range, and progress photos on a timeline with a before/after slider.
  • Lifts as a percentage of body weight, and a running total of everything you've ever lifted.
  • Edit any saved workout after the fact, log one you did on paper, or move it to the right date. Records are re-read from the corrected history.

Accounts and data

  • Passkeys (Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint) with per-profile data synced across devices. Password sign-in can be switched on per instance; new devices pair with a one-time code or QR.
  • Two devices editing at once merge field by field instead of overwriting each other (see sync).
  • Import from FitNotes, Strong, Hevy (CSV or API key) and Apple Health weight exports. Export everything as one JSON file, or your workouts and body data as a spreadsheet (CSV).
  • Share a plan as a small file or print it as a PDF.
  • Optional admin dashboard with invite-only signup and an activity log.
  • 20 languages, including right-to-left Arabic and Traditional Chinese. Exercise names and instructions are translated for most of them.

On the phone and the wrist

  • Apps for iPhone, iPad and Android that work on their own (no server, no account) or connected to yours. Rest timer in the notification shade, reminders, and Health Connect or Apple Health in both directions: workouts go out, weigh-ins and heart rate per set come back in.
  • A gym reminder, off by default: walk into one of your gyms and the phone nudges you to hit Start. Once a day at most, never after you trained, and your gyms stay on the phone.
  • An Apple Watch app: tick off sets with the Digital Crown, RPE or RIR right on the wrist, a full-screen rest countdown, heart rate per set, a Lock button against stray crown presses, and complications. No watch? AirPods Pro 3 do the heart rate on iOS 26.
  • Widgets and a Live Activity on the iPhone: log a set, skip the rest or jump to the next exercise from the Lock Screen without opening the app.

Only what you use

  • Modules: switch whole parts of the app on and off in Settings → Modules, from "Just training" to "Everything". Body, Health, Motivation, the Coach, seasonal themes and more each disappear completely while they're off, and nothing is deleted.

Optional extras, off by default

  • An AI coach that drafts a week of routines and later suggests changes based on what you logged, and answers questions about your training. You approve every change. It runs on your server, or on the phone alone, with your own provider key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Ollama included).
  • An MCP server so an assistant like Claude Desktop can answer questions about your training history, and log a workout you describe to it. Local; not part of the Docker build.
  • Integrations in one place: Apple Health, Health Connect (Garmin, Fitbit, Withings and friends come in through them), imports, and signed webhooks to Home Assistant, n8n or ntfy when you finish a workout, set a record or weigh in.

The full list of what changed release by release is in the changelog.

Quick start

You need Docker with Compose.

git clone https://github.com/DuarteSantos8/openGym
cd openGym
cp .env.example .env
docker compose pull      # prebuilt images, amd64 + arm64 (skip this to build from source)
docker compose up -d

Open http://localhost:8080, tap Create profile, and you're in. The exercise animations are part of the image, so there's nothing else to download.

To reach it from your phone with passkeys you need HTTPS on a domain; that's a two-line change in .env. The self-hosting guide walks through Cloudflare Tunnel, Caddy, Traefik and nginx, and there are separate guides for HTTPS on a LAN, a Mac with Tailscale and Kubernetes.

Note

Images are published from the same tag to ghcr.io/duartesantos8/opengym-{api,web} (what docker-compose.yml pulls) and registry.gitlab.com/duartesantos8/opengym/{api,web}. Swap the image: lines if you prefer GitLab's registry, or run docker compose up -d --build to build locally. Either way you don't need Node on the host.

Configuration reference (all through .env)
Variable What it does Default
RP_ID Hostname passkeys are bound to localhost
ORIGIN Full URL the app is served from http://localhost:8080
WEB_PORT Host port for the web UI 8080
NGINX_PORT Port the web container listens on inside the container 80
BACKEND Name of the API service that /api is proxied to api
PORT Port the API listens on; the web container proxies to the same value 3000
RP_NAME Name shown in the passkey prompt openGym
SESSION_DAYS How long a sign-in lasts, in days 90
ADMIN_UIDS User ids that get the admin dashboard, comma-separated (none)
FIRST_USER_ADMIN 1: the first profile created on an empty instance becomes its admin (off)
INVITE_ONLY Require an invite code to create a profile (off)
ALLOW_GUEST Offer "Continue without account"; 0 requires a profile (on)
PASSWORD_LOGIN Offer name-and-password sign-in next to passkeys (off)
TRUST_PROXY Let the sign-in throttle read the client address from proxy headers 1 in docker-compose.yml
AUDIT_LOG Record sign-ins and admin actions; 0 records nothing (on)
AUDIT_MAX Events kept in the activity log; 0 for no limit 5000
AUDIT_DAYS Days kept in the activity log; 0 keeps until AUDIT_MAX 90
AUDIT_IP Record the caller's address: off, net (network only) or full off
ALLOWED_PRIVATE_IPS Private addresses push endpoints may resolve to (FakeDNS, split-horizon DNS): comma-separated IPs, a-b ranges or CIDR blocks (none)
INTEGRATIONS Server integrations to offer, comma-separated: webhook (integrations) (none)
INTEGRATIONS_ALLOW_LAN 1: webhooks may reach your home network (Home Assistant), http included; never loopback (off)
VAPID_SUBJECT Contact URL sent with push notifications your ORIGIN
API_TARGET API image to build: default, or coach with the Claude Agent SDK and Codex CLI default
COACH_DISABLED 1 forces the AI coach off instance-wide (unset)

Push-notification keys are generated on first run into ./data/vapid.json. DATA_DIR is pinned to /data inside the container and mapped to ./data on the host; change the volume, not the variable. The self-hosting guide covers every option in detail.

Phone app

The same codebase builds the phone apps with Capacitor. Use them on their own (everything stays on the phone, no account) or connect them to your server and sync.

Get it
iPhone and iPad, with the Apple Watch app The App Store, in every App Store country
Android The signed APK from the latest release or opengym.ch, in three sizes: Standard (openGym-X.Y.Z.apk, animations at 180 px, about 315 MB), Plus (openGym-Plus-X.Y.Z.apk, 240 px, about 424 MB) and HD (openGym-HD-X.Y.Z.apk, 360 px, about 760 MB). It updates itself and stays the kind you picked
Google Play In closed testing: Google wants 12 testers for 14 days before it lets everyone in. Join the tester group, then opt in. It installs right over the APK and keeps your data
Wear OS watch (beta) Rides along with the Google Play test: once Google's watch review is done, "openGym Beta" shows up in the Play Store on your Galaxy Watch, Pixel Watch and friends. Details: docs/WEAR_OS.md

Every APK sits next to its .sha256. The APK and the Play app share one signing key, so you can switch between them (or between Standard, Plus and HD) without losing data. Details, building it yourself and connecting to your server: docs/MOBILE.md.

How it works

  • frontend/ is React 19 and Vite (React Router, Zustand), built to static files inside Docker.
  • api/ is plain node:http with three dependencies: @simplewebauthn/server for passkeys, web-push for notifications and undici for the AI coach's provider calls. Everything is stored as JSON under ./data.
  • web/ builds the frontend and serves it with nginx, proxying /api so the whole app sits on one origin, which passkeys require.

The architecture overview has the longer version, with diagrams of the frontend, sync, the exercise media and the watch.

The training logic (progression rules, 1RM, how a logged session is read back) lives in pure functions under frontend/src/lib/ with tests beside them. The HTTP API is documented as an OpenAPI spec in api/openapi.yaml, browsable at opengym.ch/api.html.

How sync works

Each profile's data is one document with a server revision. A device sends the revision it last saw along with its changes; if another device wrote in between, the server refuses and returns the current document so the device can merge and retry. Every change carries its own stamp, down to a single setting or routine field, so the merge keeps the newest edit of each one and a deletion stays deleted.

Nothing that hasn't reached the server is discarded on disconnect or sign-out, and the app shows a banner whenever it's working offline.

Your data

Everything lives in ./data on your host:

File Contents
db.json Profiles and public passkey data
db.json.bak A copy of the last good db.json, used if the main file can't be read
state-<user>.json Each user's plan, workouts, body weight and settings
audit.log Admin activity log (no IP addresses unless you turn that on)
secret Session-cookie signing key

Back up ./data and you've backed up everything. Passkey private keys never reach the server; they stay in your phone's secure hardware or your password manager.

Documentation

The documentation index sorts every guide by who it's for. The most used ones:

I want to Read
Get a quick answer FAQ
Set up my own instance Self-hosting
Use the Android or iPhone app Phone app
Bring my history from another app Importing data
Turn on the AI coach AI coach
Contribute code Contributing
Report a security problem Security

Roadmap

A release roughly every one to two weeks, each one whatever has passed testing by then. The full plan is in ROADMAP.md, and the issues sit in the GitHub milestones.

Release When Theme
v1.4.0 released Oct 2026 A new exercise database with 5,632 exercises, plus two rounds of community work
v1.4.1 released Oct 2026 Bug fixes for v1.4.0
v1.4.2 released Oct 2026 The App Store, the Apple Watch, widgets, three APK sizes
v1.4.3 released Oct 2026 The Halloween and community release: gym reminder, health data read back, watch upgrades, CSV export
v1.4.4 released Nov 2026 Programmes, a fresh look, Modules, a tour with tutorials, AirPods heart rate, kg or lb per exercise, the Google Play closed test and a Wear OS beta
v1.4.5 Nov 2026 Google Play for everyone, F-Droid, Settings → Integrations (Strava, webhooks, calendar, Nextcloud), timed holds that start themselves
v1.4.6 Dec 2026 Wear OS out of beta, deeper Health Connect, body composition
v1.4.7 Dec 2026 The progression engine by @giulioleuci, circuits, AMRAP and EMOM
later dates are guesses Search and catalogue, accounts, a trainer role, skins, Garmin, database storage

Community

  • Discord for release announcements, self-hosting help and quick back-and-forth. Usually the fastest way to get an answer.
  • Discussions for questions and ideas you want the next person to find by searching.
  • Issues for reproducible bugs and agreed-on work. Login trouble is almost always an RP_ID/ORIGIN mismatch; the self-hosting guide covers it.
  • Pull requests are welcome; start with CONTRIBUTING.md.

Where the code lives

GitHub is the home of the project. gitlab.com/DuarteSantos8/opengym is a mirror, updated by a GitHub Actions workflow on every push to main and every release tag. It exists because its CI builds the multi-arch images and the SBOMs for its registry (the APKs are built and signed on the release machine and attached to the GitHub release). Nothing is merged there by hand. In the changelog, !NN refers to a GitLab merge request from the weeks in August and September 2026 when the project lived there.

How openGym is built

People have asked about this, so plainly: openGym is developed with Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent. A large share of the code, tests and documentation is drafted in Claude Code sessions, and the repository carries a CLAUDE.md with the project context those sessions start from.

What that does and doesn't mean:

  • A person decides and ships. What goes in, what gets reviewed and merged, and every release are the maintainer's call. Changes are tested on a staging instance and on real phones before they are tagged.
  • Tests hold the logic in place. The training logic is covered by unit tests, and pull requests run the frontend, API and MCP suites in CI. That is the guard against plausible-looking code that is wrong, whoever or whatever wrote it.
  • The app itself doesn't need an LLM. Nothing in a default install calls an AI service. The AI coach and the MCP server are opt-in, and the coach only talks to the provider you configure, with your own key.

Community pull requests are written by their authors, with whatever tools they like, and reviewed the same way.

Sponsors

ElfHosted sponsors openGym and runs it for you if you'd rather not self-host: a managed openGym instance, built from our tagged releases with no code changes, with a 7-day trial. Your own server stays the first-class way to run openGym, and other hosts are welcome to offer it too (it's AGPL).

Sponsoring keeps the lights on. It buys no say in what openGym does: nothing is held back for sponsors, and nothing ever will be.

Support

openGym is free and stays free: AGPL, no paid tier, nothing held back for sponsors. If it replaced a paid tracker for you and you'd like to chip in, there's Buy Me a Coffee, Ko-fi and GitHub Sponsors (the app has the same three under Settings → About & updates, and on the iPhone a shortcut to leaving an App Store review). A star, a bug report or a pull request helps just as much.

The exercise media is not covered by that license. A non-commercial fork may keep them unmodified with the notice; anything else needs your own licence from gymvisual.com. The exercise text in catalogue/ is openGym's and open to contributions.

item.title: rorygallagher2024/glasshouse
item.description:
For rooted LG webOS TVs: a live dashboard, privacy control, debloating, an ad & telemetry blocker, replacement home screen, and custom screensavers. Runs on the TV itself. Includes an optional Home Assistant MQTT bridge for smart home control.

https://rorygallagher2024.github.io/glasshouse/

Glasshouse

Own the glass. A dashboard, privacy controls and Home Assistant bridge for rooted LG webOS TVs.

Note

You bought the TV.

It's your TV and you should control it. You own the glass.

Designed for those who reject their network-connected home appliances being used as a platform for advertising, telemetry and vendor-controlled experiences, this project brings control, visibility and automation back to the device.

It offers multiple ways to remove ads, withdraw from agreements and services designed to monetize your data, and make the TV a simpler, more streamlined experience — alongside a wide range of useful features, customisation and local smart-home integration.

Glasshouse itself is local, transparent, and requires no cloud service. No nonsense, no data collection, no ads, no dark patterns. I don't want your data.

Glasshouse is a server that runs directly on a rooted LG webOS TV, providing both a live browser dashboard and a dashboard app.

Use it for remote control, app installation and removal, OLED panel care, privacy controls, service menu access, and hardware telemetry. It also includes an MQTT bridge for integrating the TV with Home Assistant and other smart-home software.

Compatibility at a glance

  • webOS: 2.2 through 11 (LG's webOS 26) confirmed; tested across 2015–2026 models. Other versions likely work as well. LG names its versions two ways: webOS version numbers gives both
  • Panels: OLED (full panel wear telemetry and burn-in controls) and LCD (core dashboard, controls, and telemetry; OLED Care tab hides automatically)
  • Access: Rooted via Homebrew Channel. Telnet or SSH. No external dependencies or internet access needed on the TV
  • Tested hardware: 75 TVs across 51 series verified so far (LF632V, UF850T, UH600V, UH6030, UH610V, UH635V, B6, B7, SJ80, UJ63, B8, C8, LK61, UK63, LM57, UM71, UM73, C9, CX, GX, UN73, C1, G1, NANO75, NANO85, UP80, UP81, QNED82, UQ80, B2, C2, G2, C3, UR80, QNED80, B4, G3, C4, G4, QNED86, UT73, UT81, C5, G5, CS, LX3, UA73, UA75, C6, NU80, QNED84). Other rooted models should work; see full table

Read the documentation for the features, installation, Home Assistant and security.

Quick start

  1. Root the TV and install the Homebrew Channel.
  2. Clone this repository on a computer on the same network as the TV.
  3. Run ./deploy.sh <tv-ip> from the server/ directory.
  4. Open http://<tv-ip>:8080/ in a browser.

That's it. The dashboard is ready to use.

The installation guide has the details and troubleshooting.

What it's for

This project is intended to give a rooted webOS TV a useful local control surface instead of requiring the owner to work around the TV's built-in menus, vendor services and cloud dependencies.

  1. A cleaner Home screen. A replacement Home app with full control over what displays, and no ads, with a row of Internet TV channels from your own IPTV playlist. Or choose Glasshouse Minimal, a plainer one that comes with it, or put a launcher of your own in its place, or a web page such as a Home Assistant dashboard. Available on webOS 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11

  2. Controlling the TV without the cloud. Remote's keys, volume, inputs, power, sleep timer, comprehensive picture and sound settings, Game Optimizer, and much more.

  3. Seeing what the TV is configured to collect, and switching it off. One button to turn ads and telemetry off, including LG's content-recognition engine. Every data agreement is recorded in the app, with most of them switchable from the dashboard.

  4. App management and debloating. Install apps from the Homebrew Channel catalog, uninstall apps, disable unnecessary background system services to free up RAM and CPU cycles, stop LG keeping apps loaded in the background that are never used, and hide non-removable built-in LG system apps from LG's Home.

  5. Remapping the remote's buttons. Point Netflix, Prime Video, Guide, the color keys and the TV's other shortcut buttons at any installed app, an HDMI input or Live TV, or turn them off, or have Input open a strip of the HDMI inputs over the picture.

  6. Replacing the screen saver. Over a dozen screensavers to choose from, and customisable brightness settings.

  7. Integrating the TV with a smart home. The MQTT bridge exposes the TV as a single device with its controls and telemetry, with Home Assistant support through MQTT Discovery and the same underlying interface available to other MQTT clients. You can also send button press events to Home Assistant to control your smart home from your TV remote.

  8. Seeing what the TV is actually doing. SoC temperature, CPU load, memory, Wi-Fi signal and throughput, storage health, watch time and much more.

  9. Observing OLED panel wear. Track the lifetime use of your TV with cumulative panel hours, compensation cycle progress, Pixel Refresher countdown with scheduling, completed cycle counters and refresher failure alerts.

  10. Controlling the OLED burn-in protections. Surfaces all the burn-in protections, explains what each one does and allows you to switch them off. This includes ASBL and Global Stress Reduction which is normally reachable only from a TV's service menu with a service remote and a PIN.

  11. Opening the service menu, and unlocking it where it is locked. LG's own engineering menu, put on the TV screen from a browser which means no service remote is needed. Newer firmware shows a cut-down version of it until it is unlocked, which the dashboard can do as well.

  12. Reading all of it on the TV itself. An optional app on the home screen puts the same readings and controls on the TV, driven by the remote, for when there is no phone or laptop to hand.

  13. Managing TVs from Android. A phone app that keeps a list of TVs, shows which are online, wakes them over Wake-on-LAN, and opens each one's dashboard full screen.

Screenshots

 
Metrics and Control tabs, shown in dark and light themes.

More screenshots, including Home Assistant.

Android app

Glasshouse for Android keeps a list of TVs, shows which are online and opens each one's dashboard full screen. A TV is added by scanning any QR code on its dashboard, which carries the token as well. See the Android app documentation for more details.

It is on Google Play, for Android 10 and later. Problems and suggestions go in the app's issues.

Documentation

  • Installing and tested TVs
  • The dashboard, tab by tab
  • Home Assistant, entities and remote button events
  • Updating and uninstalling
  • Security
  • What it changes on the TV
  • Internals

The pages are built from docs/, so they can also be read there.

Security

The dashboard has no authentication by default, for frictionless control from any phone or browser on a trusted local network. Never expose port 8080 directly to the internet (do not port-forward). Security covers the token, closing the port to the network, and MQTT.

Support the project

Glasshouse is free, open-source, and maintained in spare time alongside community contributions. If it provides value to you, donations are much appreciated, helping to offset the personal cost of LLM tokens used for development and webOS research.

Disclaimer

Use this software at your own risk.

  • Root access and hardware. This runs custom software with root privileges on an embedded TV OS. It is designed to be lightweight and to leave the read-only rootfs untouched, but the author accepts no responsibility for damage, bootloops, bricked devices, voided warranties, data loss or panel issues.
  • Power and control commands. Reboot, power off, screen blanking and Pixel Refresher scheduling issue low-level luna-send calls. Understand what each does before using it.
  • Trademarks. An independent, unofficial community project, not affiliated with or endorsed by LG Electronics. webOS is a trademark of LG Electronics.
  • Fonts. Bundles Outfit and Manrope under the SIL Open Font License 1.1; licence texts ship in server/assets/fonts/.

item.title: citrolabs/ego-lite
item.description:
The fastest browser for AI agents to run browser automation, built for sharing your logged-in browser state with your AI agents, like Codex or Claude Code, without disturbing you. Zero cost, zero config.

https://lite.ego.app

The fastest browser for AI agents to run web automation

English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Português · Español · Français · Italiano · Русский

ego (lite) is a browser where you and your AI agents work in parallel. Your agents run their browser tasks in their own Spaces, isolated workspaces inside the same browser, while you keep browsing in yours, so no agent ever takes the browser away from you. And the automation itself finishes faster, on fewer tokens.

Existing tools like browser-use and agent-browser are a bridge to the browser, not a browser of their own: they need a separate one to drive, your browser data rarely carries over intact, the connection is unstable, and you and the agent end up fighting over control of the browser. ego lite is one browser designed from the start for the two of you to share. No extra setup, and the agent can always reach your real logins and tabs through ego-browser.

Demo

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ffe7954b-58ee-411e-b35d-ec30c58a08bc

Quick Start

ego lite runs on macOS and Windows, and Linux is on the roadmap.

1. Install

Pick whichever fits your flow.

1.1 Download the app

Click to download, then open it to install. Either way, ego lite adds the ego-browser skill to every agent's skills directory on your machine.

1.2 Add the skill with npx

Install just the ego-browser skill:

npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite

The first time your agent runs a browser task, it walks you through installing the ego lite app.

1.3 Let your agent set it up

Paste this into your agent:

Set up ego lite for me: https://github.com/citrolabs/ego-lite

Read `skills/ego-browser/references/install.md` and follow the steps to install ego lite.

On first launch, ego lite asks one question, whether to migrate your Chrome data. Say yes and your agent inherits your existing logins, cookies, extensions, and bookmarks.

2. Try your first task

In your agent CLI, type /ego-browser followed by a space, then describe what you want in plain language:

ego-browser follow @ego_agent on x.com for me

The agent picks up the ego-browser skill, opens the page in its own Space, reads a Snapshot (the page turned into structured text), acts on the page, and reports back, all while your own tabs stay untouched.

Your browsing data, cookies, and everything else the browser holds stay on your device. ego lite keeps its data collection deliberately narrow: simple product signals, like whether you've set ego lite as your default browser.

Highlights of ego lite

Feature What it does
Code-based, not CLI-based: faster runs on fewer tokens for complex tasks The capabilities ego lite exposes to the agent are wrapped as JavaScript functions the agent calls directly. The agent gets to do what it does best: write code, composing a multi-step task into a single output instead of getting stuck in a "call two commands, look at the result, call two more commands" loop. Compared to the conventional CLI approach, complex workflows finish far faster, with higher task success rates, far fewer tool calls per task, and a much lower cost per task.
A dedicated Space for every agent ego lite gives each agent its own fully isolated Space. You browse up front, your agent works in the background, and they don't get in each other's way. You can see which Space has an agent running at any moment, and take it over or stop it whenever you want.
Your agents multitask in Spaces, parallel workspaces inside the same browser Each Space gets its own AI agent or its own task, all running at the same time. Claude Code enriching 10 leads in 10 parallel Spaces. Codex scraping 5 competitor sites in 5 more. They don't collide or steal your tabs. Your mouse stays where you left it.
The strongest page Snapshot on the market Thanks to customization inside the browser engine, ego lite produces the highest-quality page snapshots, the view text-only models rely on to "see" and act on a webpage. It reliably handles tough cases like deeply nested iframes, exactly where other approaches consistently break down.
Any agent can drive it through ego-browser ego-browser is the connection layer between any agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or a custom one) and ego lite. It exposes the browser as a set of in-page JavaScript tools: snapshot, fill, click, wait, navigate, capture. The agent writes a JavaScript snippet calling those tools, and ego-browser runs it on the page in one pass.
Experience accumulation that makes your agent faster the more you use it (coming soon) Most of an agent's time on browser tasks goes to trial and error. ego lite's official Skill distills every successful action into reusable tools and workflows, so similar tasks down the line run up to 5x faster.

ego lite vs existing products

Most tools can automate a browser. The real questions are what browser the agent gets, whether you can keep working at the same time, and whether the tool is built for the agent you already use or a built-in one.

Feature ego lite Browser extensions
Claude/Codex in Chrome		 Built-in browsers
Claude/ChatGPT built-in browser		 Cloud browsers
Browserbase/Browser Use		 Browser CLIs
playwright-cli/Browser Harness		 AI browsers
Comet/Dia
Works with any AI agent ✓ — — ✓ ✓ —
Uses your browser logins ✓ ✓ — — — ✓
Fewer CAPTCHAs ✓ ✓ — — — ✓
Works across your whole computer ✓ — ✓ — ✓ —
Doesn't hijack your browser ✓ — ✓ ✓ — —
Parallel multitasking ✓ — — ✓ — —
Runs large scraping jobs ✓ — — ✓ ✓ —
Works as your daily browser ✓ ✓ — — — ✓
Free ✓ — — — ✓ —
Data stored locally ✓ ✓ ✓ — ✓ —
Reusable skills (coming soon) ✓ — — — — —

Benchmarks

Faster runs, higher success rates, fewer tokens. We ran ego-browser and four other browser tools for AI agents on Real-World Bench: 31 complex browser automation tasks on live websites. ego-browser leads on speed, success rate, and cost, and gets your agent through complex web tasks 47% to 63% faster than the other tools.

Every tool ran the same 31 tasks, driven by the same agent (pi) with the same model (gpt-5.6-sol, thinking effort max) and graded by the same judge against per-task rubrics. A task counts as a full success only when every requirement is met.

item.title: michael-denyer/pstack-claude
item.description:
Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, Muse, OpenCode, Pi, and Prime Agent versions of Poteto's pstack. Rigorous agent workflows with Cursor primitives translated for other harnesses.

pstack

Lauren Tan's pstack is an opinionated Cursor skill stack that improves agent outcomes. This is a port for Claude Code, Codex, Pi, GitHub Copilot, Muse, and other agent harnesses. It tracks upstream and also carries named policy forks, each declared in tools/forks.json.

Tell poteto-mode your goal and it will invoke the correct workflow for the task. It keeps your code concise, simple and verified.

For concurrency bugs and invariants that tests cannot reach, /create-formal-verification-skill picks the riskiest property in your code, verifies it with a tool that fits, and leaves a project skill the next agent reruns. The separate agent-formal-verify plugin goes deeper on the method, with guided TLA+ model checking, Lean proofs, and Kani for Rust.

Built for Claude Code

This port translates upstream's Cursor skills for Claude Code before installation. Upstream's Claude Code install asks agents to translate Cursor names at runtime, using extra tokens and relying on them to apply the mapping correctly. This port also adds a SessionStart hook that routes tasks to poteto-mode.

Install

Claude Code

Run in Claude Code 2.1.292 or later:

/plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
/plugin install pstack@pstack-claude

Claude Code leaves auto-update off for third-party marketplaces, so pstack stays on the version you installed. To turn it on, run /plugin, open the Marketplaces tab, select pstack-claude, and choose Enable auto-update. To update once by hand, run claude plugin update pstack@pstack-claude.

Codex

Run in your terminal:

codex plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
codex plugin add pstack@pstack-claude

Invoke a skill by typing $ and its name, such as $poteto-mode or $babysit, then choosing its entry, which inserts $pstack:<name>. /skills lists every skill.

Pi

Run in your terminal, with Pi 1.5.1 or later:

pi install git:github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude

The package loads the skills and the pstack Pi extension, which adds the subagent, question, and wake-up tools the skills use, plus /loop and the routing instruction. Invoke a skill with /skill:<name>.

GitHub Copilot

Run in your terminal:

copilot plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
copilot plugin install pstack@pstack-claude

This installs pstack for the Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, which share ~/.copilot. Start a new session afterwards. Copilot ships no default pstack models, so the first skill that needs one runs setup-pstack to pick from the models your account lists, and later sessions reuse that choice.

The Copilot build is tested on Copilot CLI 1.0.87 through 1.0.92. On those versions the routing hook's context reaches the session alongside other plugins' session-start context. If a later version keeps only one plugin's context, setup-pstack offers a standing instruction for ~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md instead. On 1.0.92, once the CLI caches its computer-use experiment assignment, copilot -p sessions list no plugin skills and a skill call returns "Skill not found". Interactive sessions, the hooks, and the agents are unaffected.

Muse

Run in your terminal:

git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
muse plugins install ./plugins/pstack
muse plugins approve pstack

The first command installs the native Muse plugin bundle. The second approves its SessionStart hook and agent definitions, which Muse runs only after approval. Start a new session afterwards. Invoke a skill with /<name> (for example /poteto-mode), which Muse lists for each user-invocable skill.

OMP

Run in your terminal:

omp plugin marketplace add michael-denyer/pstack-claude
omp plugin install --scope user pstack@pstack-claude

Restart OMP after installing, disabling, or uninstalling pstack. OMP 18.16.0 shares one plugin cache across scopes, so an upgrade or removal can affect other installations; inspect their source and scope before changing them. See OMP issue 16827.

Kimi Code CLI

After a release containing kimi.plugin.json is published, close other Kimi sessions and install it in a fresh Kimi Code CLI session:

/plugins install https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
/reload

To test an unreleased checkout, use /plugins install /absolute/path/to/pstack-claude instead, followed by /reload; Kimi copies the whole checkout, including Git metadata and local files, so use a clean, reviewed copy. To update, close other Kimi sessions, reinstall from the same source in a fresh session, and run /reload. Invoke a skill as /skill:pstack:poteto-mode; see the Kimi mapping for tool guidance.

Grok Build 
git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
grok plugin install "$PWD/plugins/pstack" --trust
grok plugin enable pstack

Start a new session and use /poteto-mode to load the skill explicitly. To update a local install, quit Grok sessions, inspect grok plugin details pstack and back up any edits in the installed copy, pull the checkout, run grok plugin uninstall pstack --keep-data, and repeat the last two commands. If pstack was disabled, disable it again before restarting. grok plugin update does not refresh a local install.

MiniMax Code

For a first install, check that ${MINIMAX_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.minimax}/plugins/pstack does not already exist. Then run in your terminal:

git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
mkdir -p "${MINIMAX_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.minimax}/plugins"
cp -R plugins/pstack "${MINIMAX_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.minimax}/plugins/pstack"

MiniMax Code loads each directory under plugins/ in its data directory as a local plugin, and reads pstack through its Claude Code reader with the skills, agents, and routing hook. mcode plugin list shows it as pstack@local. To update, record its enabled state, quit every mcode process, and move plugins/pstack to an unused path outside plugins/. Run git pull and the cp line again. Check mcode plugin list and restore the previous enabled state if needed.

OpenCode 2

Clone the repository, then add the absolute path to plugins/pstack/opencode to the existing plugins array in ~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc. On Windows, use a path such as C:/Users/name/pstack-claude/plugins/pstack/opencode. Restart OpenCode after checkout updates.

Alternatively, install, check, or update the native Git package:

opencode plugin add 'github:michael-denyer/pstack-claude#main'
opencode plugin check 'github:michael-denyer/pstack-claude#main'
opencode plugin update 'github:michael-denyer/pstack-claude#main'

A commit-pinned reference does not advance. If a check immediately after installation reports no package plugins, wait for the server to load it and check again.

If you previously installed pstack skills into ~/.agents/skills, inspect the links and remove only those pointing to your pstack checkout before using the plugin.

The plugin registers pstack- skill IDs and adds routing in root sessions. If routing is missing, run opencode api get /api/skill and check that each pstack- path belongs to this plugin. Resolve any conflicting skill before manually invoking that ID. Use session hook: off in the OpenCode model sheet to disable routing. To remove the plugin, remove its configured path and restart the service, or use opencode plugin remove with the exact Git specifier. OpenCode 1 is unsupported. See the OpenCode mapping.

Antigravity (agy)

Run in your terminal:

git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
agy plugin install ./plugins/pstack

This installs the native Antigravity plugin bundle (skills, agents, and SessionStart routing hook) into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/pstack.

Other harnesses

Gemini CLI, Prime Agent, and skills-only Codex installs read skills from ~/.agents/skills/. Run in your terminal:

git clone https://github.com/michael-denyer/pstack-claude
cd pstack-claude
mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills
for s in plugins/pstack/skills/*/; do
  target=~/.agents/skills/"$(basename "$s")"
  test -e "$target" || test -L "$target" || ln -s "$(pwd)/$s" "$target"
done

To update, run git pull in the clone, then run the for loop again to link skills added since the last run. These installs have no routing hook, so ask for poteto-mode by name or add a standing instruction to the harness's instruction file. See shared installation for per-harness notes and uninstalling.

Configure

pstack provides automatic routing on Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Muse, MiniMax Code, Antigravity, Pi, Kimi Code CLI, OMP, and OpenCode 2. The runtimes deliver the instruction at different points: Kimi adds it while the plugin is enabled, OMP adds it before each main-agent turn, and OpenCode adds it at each model step in root sessions. Grok Build exposes a routing hint through a skill description; the model may not follow it. Codex requires hook trust through /hooks, and Muse requires muse plugins approve pstack. Other harnesses have no automatic routing.

Run setup-pstack to turn automatic routing on or off, change model defaults, or set a reasoning effort per role (arena runners: opus @xhigh, fable @max). On OMP, the session hook setting applies globally across profiles; on Kimi, enable or disable the plugin to control routing. See the routing reference.

Getting started

Use poteto-mode to fix the search filter resetting when I change pages.

For a bug, it reproduces the failure, uses how and why to investigate, delegates the fix, then reruns the failing case. If the fix crosses a function boundary, it brings in architect before implementation. You receive the fix and the failing and passing evidence.

A localized bug with a demonstrated cause can use the focused-fix exception. One delegate investigates and implements the correction when it preserves existing interfaces and state semantics and has a focused regression check. Reproduction, verification, and required independent review still apply; a small patch alone does not qualify.

Other playbooks cover planning, features, refactoring, performance issues, investigations, prototypes, PR maintenance, shipping, and longer projects.

Details

  • Skills and slash commands
  • Runtime setup
  • Models and dependencies
  • Maintenance and port scope

Data handling

pstack has no server or telemetry. Anything its skills ask your agent to read, including session transcripts, goes to your model provider. Scripts run locally, and PR tools use your GitHub CLI login.

This port has no automatic agent-diary reporting or diary opt-in setting. For a local decision trail, ask for show-me-your-work. Longer or unattended workflows also invoke it. The trail stays uncommitted by default. If the trail is committed and pushed to a shared PR, anyone with access to the PR can read it.

To share feedback, submit a short, manually reviewed report through GitHub issues. Include the pstack version, runtime, relevant workflow, and observed result. Remove credentials, customer data, private repository links, and sensitive log or configuration values before posting; share a summary instead of raw transcripts.

Contributing

Thanks for helping make this port better. Bug reports, documentation fixes, and runtime improvements are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the checks and where your change belongs. Report vulnerabilities privately as described in SECURITY.md.

To support maintenance of this port, buy the maintainer a coffee.

License

This port, including its modifications and additions, is also MIT-licensed, © 2026 Michael Denyer. Original pstack © 2026 Lauren Tan; imported cursor-team-kit and thermos skills © 2026 Cursor. See LICENSE-cursor-team-kit, LICENSE-thermos, and NOTICE.md.

item.description:
JavaScript 3D Library.

https://threejs.org/

three.js

JavaScript 3D library

The aim of the project is to create an easy-to-use, lightweight, cross-browser, general-purpose 3D library. The current builds only include WebGL and WebGPU renderers but SVG and CSS3D renderers are also available as addons.

Usage

This code creates a scene, a camera, and a geometric cube, and it adds the cube to the scene. It then creates a WebGL renderer for the scene and camera, and it adds that viewport to the document.body element. Finally, it animates the cube within the scene for the camera.

import * as THREE from 'three';

const width = window.innerWidth, height = window.innerHeight;

// init

const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera( 70, width / height, 0.01, 10 );
camera.position.z = 1;

const scene = new THREE.Scene();

const geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry( 0.2, 0.2, 0.2 );
const material = new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial();

const mesh = new THREE.Mesh( geometry, material );
scene.add( mesh );

const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer( { antialias: true } );
renderer.setSize( width, height );
renderer.setAnimationLoop( animate );
document.body.appendChild( renderer.domElement );

// animation

function animate( time ) {

	mesh.rotation.x = time / 2000;
	mesh.rotation.y = time / 1000;

	renderer.render( scene, camera );

}
